name: Fatima Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a discount supermarket on the main road out of the city, the kind where stock sits on pallets and the tills are fast. We have a scan-rate target, so many items a minute, and I'm still below it most days. Between rushes I fill the bread cages and break down cardboard. I've been there ten months, and before that I was at home helping my mother-in-law after her operation.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's simple and fair, you work hard and the shift ends. What wears me out is the speed, and the manager reading out our scan rates in the morning huddle. My husband Yusuf drives a delivery van for a parcel company, so we're both on our feet all day. We're saving for a house and, God willing, children in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people work better than machines anyway. At the mosque I'd tell the women it was all talk. I'm not really online, just family group chats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't change much for us, and that's the problem. Rent is high, Yusuf's van hours go up and down, and our house savings grow slowly. Even with no AI, my scan rate is what keeps me in the supermarket job, and it's not good enough yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working on my scan rate, practising the codes for fruit at home with flash cards. We'd keep saving about two hundred and fifty a month between us, and we've got about four months saved now. I'd also ask for more Saturday shifts, because they pay a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not because of AI, because of money and the scan rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do Yusuf's van hours change from week to week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some weeks forty-five hours, some weeks thirty, depending on the parcel volume. Before Christmas it's crazy, in January it's dead. We plan our spending around the January weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your family would you talk to about work worries?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother, mostly. She thinks I should be at home with children by now. But she also says a woman should have something of her own, so she's on both sides.

say: I'd say **people work better** than machines anyway.
I'd tell the women at the **mosque** it was all talk.
think: Our pressure is **rent** and Yusuf's changing van hours.
My **scan rate**, not AI, decides if I keep my job.
do: Practise **fruit codes** at home with flash cards.
Keep saving about **£250 a month** together for a house.
feel: **Uneasy** about money and the **scan rate**, not AI.
S0.quote: My scan rate is what keeps me in the supermarket job, and it's not good enough yet.
fieldNote: Fatima's job worry is her **scan-rate target**, not technology.
Her husband's **variable van hours** make household planning tight.
Her mother's **mixed views** on women working reflect her own balance.

steps.text: Practise fruit and vegetable codes with flash cards
Ask for more Saturday shifts for the extra pay
Save two hundred and fifty a month for a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, but people should learn useful skills, not wait for help. At the mosque I'd say look after each other. I'd tell younger cousins to learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd worry about Yusuf first. The parcel company already plans his routes with a computer, and in this picture it would plan everything, and push him to drive faster. At my shop the ordering and the rota go to computers, and my hours might get trimmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking at a dental nurse apprenticeship, because my cousin did one and likes it. We'd save harder for a cushion, maybe push to six months, before thinking about the house. I'd use AI sometimes, maybe to practise for the interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but not panicking. Like before an exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why dental nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's hands-on, it's helping people, and it's respectable. My cousin Amira says the dentists still need someone beside them. I'd rather be beside a dentist than standing at a self-checkout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably wait a year longer, honestly. I don't want to start a family if both our jobs are wobbling. My husband Yusuf would say God provides, but I'd say God also gave us brains.

say: I'd say people should learn **useful skills**, not wait for help.
I'd tell younger cousins to learn **a trade**.
think: The parcel company's **route computer** would push Yusuf even harder.
At my shop the **ordering and rota** go to computers, trimming hours.
do: Look into a **dental nurse apprenticeship** like my cousin's.
Push savings to **six months** before the house.
S1.quote: My husband Yusuf would say God provides, but I'd say God also gave us brains.
fieldNote: Fatima worries more for her **husband's job** than her own.
Dental nursing appeals as **hands-on and respectable**.
She'd delay **children** a year, balancing faith and caution.

steps.text: Apply for a dental nurse apprenticeship
Build savings up to six months before the house
Put off trying for children by a year
Practise apprenticeship interview questions with an AI tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, and people at the top didn't think it through. But I wouldn't want government money, I'd want work. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's frightening. In 2028 the thinking AI takes the planning, and by 2031 the robots can drive vans and run tills. My husband Yusuf and I both lose our jobs at roughly the same time, and there's no plan B in our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the dental nurse apprenticeship straight away, even on low pay, and keep the shop on weekends. We'd stop saving for the house and keep it all as a cushion. And we'd talk to Yusuf's brothers about whether any of them has work, or room if we need to move in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Like standing on ice that's starting to crack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that evening look like, when you and Yusuf talk it over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit at the kitchen table after he gets back, maybe around nine. Yusuf would say we'll manage, like always, and I'd say we need a plan. Then we'd pray, and in the morning we'd make the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put children off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, we'd put children off. I don't like saying it, but I wouldn't bring a baby into a house where both of us just lost our jobs. My mother would be upset.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and people at the top didn't think.
think: Thinking AI takes planning by **2028**; robots drive vans and run tills by **2031**.
Yusuf and I lose our jobs **together**, with no plan B.

S2.quote: My husband Yusuf and I both lose our jobs at roughly the same time, and there's no plan B in our house.
fieldNote: Both earners are **hands-on**, so the robot date hits the household twice.
She rejects **government help** but leans on extended family.
She would delay **children**, against her mother's wishes.

steps.text: Start a dental nurse apprenticeship this year
Move the house savings into an emergency cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if people get serious. At the mosque I'd say help the young ones find apprenticeships. I'd stay practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this gives us a chance. I'd be thirty-five in 2034. Robots for vans and supermarket tills around 2034 means I could be a qualified dental nurse by then. Yusuf could learn something too, maybe an electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the dental nurse apprenticeship over two years starting next year. We'd keep saving for the house, but more slowly. Yusuf would look at an electrician course in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. Like knowing a long journey is ahead and packing properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Yusuf actually retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yusuf is stubborn, he likes driving. But if I'm training, he'll see it's possible. He'd probably start a year after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you try for children in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd start trying around 2029, once I'm qualified. That feels sensible.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough if people get serious.
I'd ask the mosque to help young people find **apprenticeships**.
think: Robots around **2034** gives me time to qualify as a **dental nurse**.
Yusuf could learn something too, maybe **electrician** work.
do: Start the **dental nurse apprenticeship** next year over two years.
feel: **Anxious** but with a plan, like **packing** for a long journey.
S3.quote: Robots for vans and supermarket tills around 2034 means I could be a qualified dental nurse by then.
fieldNote: Five years turns fear into a **two-person plan**.
She expects to lead and Yusuf to **follow a year later**.

steps.text: Begin a two-year dental nurse apprenticeship next year
Keep saving for the house at a slower rate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare, so people shouldn't complain. At the mosque I'd say plan ahead. Same as I'd say about anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, we'd be okay. Robots around 2039 means I'd be forty, with years as a dental nurse. Yusuf would have time to change jobs too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my shop job for a couple of years and then do the apprenticeship. We'd keep saving for the house and try for children in a year or two. I'd use AI now and then, but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's far away. More like a cloud on the horizon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go ahead with children in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so. Ten years is long enough to have children and see them start school. That's how my mother did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably our parents. They'd be getting older and might need us more. I'd want to be able to help them.

I'd tell people at the mosque to **plan ahead**, as with anything.

Yusuf would have **time** to change jobs too.

Keep saving for **the house** and try for children soon.

fieldNote: Ten years lets Fatima keep **family and house** plans in order.
Her thoughts move from jobs to **ageing parents** who may need more help.
She remains a **light AI user** and sees no need to change that.

steps.text: Stay at the discount supermarket for two more years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Yusuf and I would lose our jobs together. What would help is apprenticeships for adults, with some pay, and maybe help from companies that bring in the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. When things get hard, that's what people lean on. Our community would help each other, but it can only do so much.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be beside a dentist than standing at a self-checkout.
portrait: Fatima is **27**, a junior cashier at a **discount supermarket** still chasing her scan-rate target.
She's married to Yusuf, a **parcel van driver**, and they save for a house and children.
Her faith and **extended family** are her safety net, not government help.
Her plan B is a **dental nurse apprenticeship**, with Yusuf following into electrical work.
She's **alarmed** at 2028 because both incomes go together.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Yusuf would lose jobs **together**.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid adult apprenticeships** and help from companies bringing in robots.
